ground_truth.title: Who's Reading Your Newsletter? Increasingly, Not a Human.
ground_truth.author: Florent Daudens
ground_truth.main_content:
An AI reads my email now, which is bliss. But I also feel conflicted about what it means for newsletters.

I haven’t opened Gmail in three weeks. My AI assistant checks it for me.

Then, I started to notice my skin is glowing. Ok, maybe not. But work life without Gmail? Highly recommended.

A few weeks ago, I connected my Gmail to my AI assistant ( I wrote about setting up here ) through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration. It’s not complicated: a Google Workspace connector that lets Claude access my inbox, calendar, and contacts the same way any app would, except through a conversational interface instead of the web interface we all know. The MCP server runs locally.

Every morning, I run a skill called “/goodmorning” (very poetic). Among other things, it spins up a subagent that scans everything that came in overnight: the newsletters, the cold outreach, the meeting confirmations, the invoices, the Slack notification emails, the “quick question” from someone who definitely doesn’t have a quick question.

It gives me a summary: here are the 4 things that actually need your attention today. Here’s a draft reply for the urgent one. Another 5-8 get tagged as “worth knowing about but no action needed”. The rest can wait.

The skill also pulls in the latest news relevant to my work, trending research papers, and saved bookmarks. I’m also dogfooding what we’re building at Mizal: a feed of what the creators and experts I follow are talking about today, surfaced by my assistant (ping me if you want early access!)

That’s it. I never see the other 80+ emails. They exist somewhere in Gmail’s servers, technically unread, and I have never been happier. Because I'm Worth It ™.

The Numbers Are Absurd

I knew email was a time sink. I didn’t realize how much until I measured it.

The average worker receives 117 emails per day and gets interrupted every 2 minutes

Email alone consumes 28% of the workweek: 11 hours, more than a full working day

68% of employees say they can’t keep up with the pace and volume

I was spending roughly two hours a day on email. Now I chat about it with my assistant, we collaborate on drafts to respond to what matters. That’s a net gain of over an hour and a half, every day, that I now spend on work that actually moves things forward.

But Here’s Where It Gets Complicated

I run a startup that helps people discover the creators they’ll love, and helps content creators become discoverable in AI conversations. A lot of those creators are newsletter writers. And here I am, telling you that I’ve essentially automated away the act of reading newsletters.

So I started digging into the data. Is this just me, or is something bigger shifting?

The newsletter industry has never been healthier, on paper:

Substack has 35 million active subscriptions, 5 million of them paid, and the CEO is targeting 50 million paid subscribers.

Beehiiv sent 28 billion emails in 2025, reaching 255 million unique readers. Paid subscription revenue on beehiiv alone hit $19 million last year, up 138% from 2024.

(The broader creator economy is a $250 billion market headed toward $480 billion by 2027, according to Goldman Sachs)

Publishers and media organizations have also jumped on the train for a long time and are doubling down on newsletters as their primary hedge against platform dependency and AI eating search traffic. The data is from mid 2024, but still interesting:

The Guardian US added 680,000 newsletter subscribers in a single year.

Axios is running 45% open rates and just launched a $1,000/year paid membership tier built entirely from a free newsletter.

I’ve seen it firsthand in my former newsroom managing roles. The email list is the one asset publishers actually own, and a newsletter is one of the best ways to build direct relationship with audience.

Newsletters are booming. More people are writing them, more people are paying for them, and media organizations are betting their survival on them.

But the delivery mechanism, the inbox, is collapsing under its own weight:

376 billion emails are sent every day globally. Half of them spam, the other half increasingly feeling like it.

51% of people unsubscribe from newsletters simply because they get too many.

Newsletters are the best distribution channel creators, media and marketers have ever had. But the channel itself could be drowning.

Inbox fatigue has been building for years. I’ll admit I’m part of the problem — I hoard newsletter subscriptions like browser tabs. But I also stopped counting how many times I clicked unsubscribe, only to keep getting unwanted emails. At some point I stopped fighting it and just let it pile up.

What This Means for Newsletter Writers?

If you depend on email to reach your audience, this shift should matter to you. Not because newsletters are dying (unlike the click, as I recently argued ). They’re not. But because the assumption underneath the entire model is shifting.

The assumption: a human opens your email, scans the subject line, reads (or skims) the content, and decides to engage.

The emerging reality: increasingly, an AI layer sits between your newsletter and the human. Maybe it’s a tool like mine. Maybe it’s Google’s CC, a Gemini-powered agent that connects to your Gmail and sends you a daily “Your Day Ahead” briefing. Maybe it’s Gmail’s new AI Inbox, which replaces your chronological email list with a briefing of what matters. Maybe it’s Apple Intelligence summarizing emails on the lock screen. Maybe it’s a Superhuman-style agent that pre-triages everything.

In every case, your newsletter has to pass through an intermediary that optimizes for one thing: is this relevant to this specific person right now?

That intermediary doesn’t care about your subject line tricks. It doesn’t respond to urgency cues or FOMO. It evaluates the actual content against what it knows about the reader’s interests, current projects, and priorities. It’s the first reader you’ll have to pass.

My hunch is that the newsletters most likely to survive AI triage or real human interest are the ones with genuine signal. Unique analysis. Original reporting. Information the reader can’t easily get elsewhere.

The ones most likely to get filtered out? The aggregators, the “weekly roundups” of links the reader has already seen, the content-marketing-disguised-as-insight.

I come back to this article I wrote a few months ago: The more I watch how AI reshuffles the media, the clearer it becomes that the fight is really about two things: platform control and coverage depth.

But I could be wrong. Maybe AI triage ends up favouring recency, or brevity, or some other signal I’m not thinking of.

This is, in a way, good news for serious newsletter writers. AI triage might actually increase engagement with high-quality newsletters by clearing out the noise around them. If my inbox goes from 90 emails to 5 important ones, and your newsletter is consistently one of the 5, that’s a much better position than competing for attention in a cluttered inbox of 90.

But if your newsletter is in the 85 that gets filtered? You just lost your reader without ever knowing it.

The Bigger Shift

The inbox was never a great content distribution system. It was just the best one available: a direct line to someone’s attention, which is the most valuable real estate in media. But that direct line only works if someone’s actually there, reading each email.

If an AI is doing the reading, the inbox becomes what it probably should have been all along: infrastructure, not interface.

For publishers and creators, this means the competitive advantage shifts from distribution (can you reach someone’s inbox?) to signal quality (can you survive their AI filter?). Getting into the inbox was the hard part. Now staying in the human’s attention is.

That’s the question I’m obsessed with: what happens when AI intermediates discovery and decides what deserves human attention? We need to think about how creators and publishers become discoverable in AI conversations in ChatGPT, Claude and the likes, be it from a website, a short video or a newsletter.

What I’d Tell Newsletter Writers

If you’re writing a newsletter today, as I am, here’s what I’d think about:

Your real audience is becoming two audiences. The human who reads your work, and the AI that decides whether to surface it. How can you be so interesting that a human reader will still want to read you? And how can you signal to an AI reader that you’re delivering value to the human behind it?

Engagement metrics will become increasingly unreliable. Open and click rates will become less relevant when an AI reads your inbox. When my assistant calls the MCP server, does it count as an open?

The newsletters that survive AI triage share one trait: they contain something the reader can’t get elsewhere. Original analysis. A distinctive perspective. A voice. If your newsletter is primarily aggregation, you’re competing against something that does aggregation infinitely better than you do.

Five Weeks In

I’m not going back to checking my inbox. The cognitive relief alone is worth it - the low-grade anxiety of the “1269” unread count, the compulsive checking (a hard habit to abandon), the context-switching tax. All gone.

But I’m also aware of what I might be missing. The serendipitous discovery in a newsletter I wouldn’t have opened or the human messiness of an unfiltered inbox that occasionally surfaces something unexpected.

I’ve traded serendipity for focus. Most days, that feels like an excellent deal. Some days, I wonder what I’m not seeing. But I can find it elsewhere.

For now, though, I’ll take the 90 minutes back. And I hope that you’ll be reading this through your own inbox or through an AI that flagged it as relevant.
